questions.stem: In which direction do particles diffuse?

options.text: From where they are crowded to where they are scarce
options.explanation: Diffusion carries particles from high concentration to low concentration until the spread is even.

options.text: From low concentration to high concentration
options.explanation: Random motion cannot build a crowd; particles drift away from crowded regions.

options.text: They do not move at all unless heated
options.explanation: Diffusion happens on its own; heating only makes it faster.

options.text: They move only downwards under gravity
options.explanation: Random motion drives the spread, not gravity; bromine climbed into the upper jar.

questions.stem: Why does diffusion happen faster at higher temperatures?

options.text: Because the particles have more kinetic energy and move more quickly
options.explanation: Hotter particles carry more kinetic energy, so their random motion spreads them sooner.

options.text: Because the particles become smaller when heated
options.explanation: Particle size never changes with temperature; only the speed of motion does.

options.text: Because heat creates extra particles to spread
options.explanation: Heating adds energy, not particles.

options.text: Because heating widens the gaps between particles permanently
options.explanation: The cause is the faster motion of the particles, not a lasting change in spacing.

questions.stem: In the bromine jar demonstration, what allows the air and bromine particles to mix?

options.text: The random motion of both kinds of particle and the large gaps between them
options.explanation: The explanation is random movement combined with the large spaces between gas particles.

options.text: The jars are shaken to stir the gases together
options.explanation: No stirring occurs; the gases mix on their own.

options.text: Bromine particles are lighter, so they float upward
options.explanation: Both gases move randomly in all directions; no floating mechanism is involved.

options.text: A chemical reaction between air and bromine
options.explanation: The gases simply mix physically; no reaction takes place.

questions.stem: Why is diffusion slower in liquids than in gases?

options.text: Because liquid particles are closely packed together and move more slowly
options.explanation: Close packing and slower movement make the spread of particles slower in liquids.

options.text: Because liquids contain no moving particles at all
options.explanation: Liquid particles move randomly and slide over each other, so diffusion still occurs.

options.text: Because liquid particles are larger than gas particles
options.explanation: Particle size does not differ between states; packing and speed do.

options.text: Because diffusion is impossible in liquids
options.explanation: Diffusion happens in both gases and liquids, only at different rates.

questions.stem: What does the potassium manganate(VII) demonstration show about diffusion in liquids?

options.text: That dissolved particles spread through the water until the colour is even, though slowly
options.explanation: The purple colour spreads through the water over time as particles mix by random motion.

options.text: That the purple colour appears only at the surface of the water
options.explanation: The colour spreads throughout the available space, not just the surface.

options.text: That the crystals dissolve without any particles moving
options.explanation: Dissolving and spreading are themselves particle motion; nothing stays fixed.

options.text: That diffusion in liquids is faster than in gases
options.explanation: The comparison runs the other way: liquids are the slower medium.

questions.stem: What happens to the solute particles when a solution is diluted?

options.text: They are still present in the solution but more spread out
options.explanation: Dilution spreads the particles through more solvent without removing any of them.

options.text: Some of them are removed along with the extra water
options.explanation: Dilution does not remove particles; it only spreads them out.

options.text: They break apart into smaller particles
options.explanation: The particles remain whole; only their spacing changes.

options.text: They clump together and sink to the bottom
options.explanation: Dilution spreads particles apart; nothing in the process makes them clump.

questions.stem: Why does the colour fade only gradually over many dilutions?

options.text: Because even a small crystal contains a very large number of very small particles
options.explanation: The long-lasting colour shows there are a lot of particles in a small amount of the substance.

options.text: Because the water permanently stains the container
options.explanation: The fading happens in the solution itself, not in the container.

options.text: Because new dye particles are created at each step
options.explanation: Dilution creates nothing; the same particles simply spread further.

options.text: Because the particles lose their colour as they spread
options.explanation: The particles keep their properties; the colour looks fainter only because they are more spread out.

questions.stem: A student adds water to a coloured solution and expects the colour to vanish at once. What does the experiment actually show?

options.text: The colour becomes fainter with each dilution and persists through many of them
options.explanation: The colour fades but does not disappear until a lot of dilutions have been done.

options.text: The colour disappears completely after a single dilution
options.explanation: That is exactly what the experiment contradicts.

options.text: The colour becomes darker as more water is added
options.explanation: Adding solvent lowers the concentration, so the colour lightens.

options.text: The colour changes from purple to blue
options.explanation: The note describes gradual fading, not a change of hue.

questions.stem: What do diffusion and dilution experiments together provide evidence for?

options.text: The kinetic theory of matter: all matter is made of tiny, moving particles
options.explanation: The exam hint names diffusion and dilution as evidence for the kinetic theory of matter.

options.text: That particles exist only in coloured solutions
options.explanation: The evidence covers solids, liquids and gases, as the opening of the note states.

options.text: That energy must always be added for particles to move
options.explanation: Diffusion happens on its own, with no energy input required.

options.text: That particles are at their largest in gases
options.explanation: Neither experiment fixes particle size by state; both depend on motion and spacing.

questions.stem: Which addition of water would make the purple colour faintest after a single dilution?

options.text: The largest volume of water, spreading the particles the most
options.explanation: More solvent means a lower concentration, so the biggest dilution gives the faintest colour.

options.text: The smallest volume of water
options.explanation: A small addition changes the concentration the least.

options.text: No water at all, as standing still dilutes best
options.explanation: Dilution specifically means adding solvent; standing changes nothing about the concentration.

options.text: Warming the solution instead of adding water
options.explanation: Warming speeds diffusion, but dilution means adding solvent to lower the concentration.
